content.intro: This lesson studies The ref() API within Vue Reactivity System. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Reactivity is the engine behind live search, totals, dependent fields, and predictable UI updates.

content_blocks.title: The ref() API: Reactive dependency flow
content_blocks.alt_text: Reactive dependency flow diagram for lesson 31: The ref() API. Change a ref or reactive property → Track dependencies; derive or run side effects → Vue schedules the required render update
content_blocks.caption: Reactivity flow: track the state that changes, choose computed values for pure derivation, and use watchers for side effects.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Vue 3 reactivity tracks dependencies in refs and reactive objects; computed values derive state, while watchers perform side effects. This lesson focuses on The ref() API. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Creating reactive references
items.text: For Creating reactive references, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

items.title: Refs for primitive and object values
items.text: For Refs for primitive and object values, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

content_blocks.code:
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
const count = ref(0)
function increment() { count.value += 1 }
</script>
<template><button @click="increment">{{ count }}</button></template>
content_blocks.expected_output: The button begins at 0 and increments. In a template, refs are automatically unwrapped; in script, read/write .value.

content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Reading and updating .value”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.
